svg.text: From a number to light: how a reply finds its way into your server
Addresses and ports are just numbers in a header. Hardware turns them into light, and a switch turns them into a specific socket.
The reply from github, arriving back at host A (image 2), followed down to the hardware:
A → E below. Letters, not numbers, so they don't mix with the trip steps of images 1 and 2.
A packet = a row of bits.
the physical address of the server

text.tspan: Each layer is read by a different thing, outside → in.
Port 443 is not a hole in anything: it's a number meaning "the HTTPS program" (51000 = the program on your side that asked).

svg.text: destination 10.20.33.10 as 32 pulses · 1 = laser flash · 0 = dark

text.tspan: a 100 Gb/s link carries 100 billion bits per second. A full 1,500-byte packet passes in ~0.12 µs.
real fast links use several brightness levels per pulse and add error-checking bits, but the idea is the same.

svg.text: it up in a table, and
fiber cable to host A's Nitro card ↓
This is where a number becomes a specific socket.
Each layer only reads its own
your VPC address, your VM never
a number in the IP header → picks the machine / VM
a number in the TCP header → picks the program
a hole in the switch's metal → picks the cable
Simplified. The outer address 10.0.4.17 and socket numbers are illustrative.
